title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
blurb: Transformers are the reliable earner here - the turns-ratio formula and a step-up/step-down calculation appear in most sessions, usually alongside a field-line drawing.
formulas: input voltage ÷ output voltage = primary turns ÷ secondary turns
input voltage × input current = output voltage × output current

items.q: State the formula linking input voltage, output voltage and the turns ratio of a transformer.
a: input (primary) voltage ÷ output (secondary) voltage = number of primary turns ÷ number of secondary turns
(Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns)
items.tip: Keep primary on top on both sides, or secondary on top on both sides. Mixing them up is the usual mistake.

items.q: Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil / the output voltage of the transformer.
items.rx: (number of turns on the secondary|output voltage (of|for) (the|this) transformer|input voltage of this transformer)
a: Substitute into Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns;
rearrange for the unknown;
evaluate - and check it makes sense (a step-up transformer must give more turns and more volts on the secondary).
items.tip: For an ideal transformer, power in = power out, so if the voltage is stepped up the current is stepped down.

items.q: State the name given to this type of transformer.
a: Step-up if the secondary has more turns and the output voltage is higher;
step-down if the secondary has fewer turns and the output voltage is lower.

items.q: Explain the operation of a step-down transformer.
a: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field;
the (soft) iron core carries this changing magnetic field to the secondary coil;
the changing magnetic field induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil;
the secondary coil has fewer turns than the primary, so the output voltage is lower than the input voltage;
a transformer will not work with a steady direct current, because that gives a constant magnetic field with no change to induce a voltage.
items.tip: The word 'changing' must appear. A magnetic field that is merely present induces nothing.

items.q: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the national grid at very high voltage.
a: For a given power, a higher voltage means a smaller current (P = I × V);
the power wasted as heat in the cables is I² × R, so a smaller current wastes much less energy;
this makes transmission more efficient (and thinner, cheaper cables can be used).
items.tip: Step-up transformers raise the voltage leaving the power station; step-down transformers lower it again before it reaches homes.

items.q: Describe the construction of an electromagnet.
a: A length of insulated wire wound into a coil (solenoid);
wrapped around a soft iron core;
connected to a d.c. supply, so that a current flows and produces a magnetic field.
items.tip: Ways to make it stronger: more turns on the coil, a larger current, or an iron core. Soft iron is used because it loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

items.q: Describe a method to show the shape and direction of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.
items.rx: (shape and direction|magnetic field).{0,60}bar magnet|plotting compass|iron filings
a: Place the magnet on a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings over it (tapping the paper) to show the shape of the field;
use a plotting compass to show the direction: place it near the magnet and mark the position of the needle ends with dots;
move the compass so it starts where the last dot was and repeat, then join the dots into a smooth field line;
repeat from several starting points to build up the pattern.
items.tip: Iron filings alone show shape but not direction. The direction mark requires the plotting compass.

items.q: Draw the magnetic field lines around the bar magnet(s).
a: Lines run from the north pole to the south pole, with arrows on them showing that direction;
lines are closest together where the field is strongest (at the poles);
lines are smooth curves and never cross or touch.

items.q: Draw an arrow to show the direction of the force on the current-carrying wire.
items.rx: direction of the force on the (wire|proton|conductor)
a: Use Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = magnetic Field (N to S), second finger = Current (+ to −), thumb = Force (motion);
the force is perpendicular to both the current and the field.
items.tip: Reversing either the current or the magnetic field reverses the force. Reversing both leaves it unchanged.

items.q: Explain how a voltage is induced when the wire is moved in the magnetic field, and how to increase it.
a: Moving the wire makes it cut through the magnetic field lines;
this induces a voltage (e.m.f.) across the wire, and a current flows if the circuit is complete;
to increase the induced voltage: move the wire faster, use a stronger magnet, or wind the wire into a coil with more turns;
if the wire is stationary or moves parallel to the field lines, no lines are cut and no voltage is induced.
